name: Yara Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy furniture and homeware for Oakfield Home Supplies, a distributor that sells to independent shops and garden centres. Sofas, lamps, kitchen sets, that sort of thing. I ran a homeware shop floor for thirty years until it closed, and I moved into buying five years ago, so I'm still the junior beside Beatrice, our senior buyer. I spend my days on supplier catalogues, sample requests and shipping dates.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I enjoy picking what will sell. I'm usually right about colours, which makes up for being slow on the spreadsheets. I use a translation tool and sometimes an AI helper to write to suppliers abroad. My husband Marcus works at a pharmacy and our kids, Tiago and Lia, are grown. We've got savings and I'd like to stop around 64.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. This one is called AI Plateau. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it sounds sensible. A plateau means more of the same, and after thirty years in homeware I know exactly how to do more of the same. At work I'd say keep using what helps and ignore the noise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm calm. The tools save me a bit on supplier emails and my job stays as it is. I'm junior but I'm steady, and the money's good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going. I'd use the translation tool more and maybe let the helper draft my sample requests. I'd ask Beatrice if she wants a shortlist method I use for colours, because it saves her time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels comfortable, not exciting. I'm happy with comfortable at 58.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything still worrying you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A worry I have, regardless of AI, is shops closing. My customers are small independents, and if more of them fold, I have fewer people to sell to. That's a bigger risk than any robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check with the sales team which of our shops are in trouble, and buy a bit more carefully. It's old-fashioned prudence.

say: I'd say it sounds **sensible**, so keep what helps and ignore the noise.
I'd say a plateau just means **more of the same**.
think: I'm **calm**, since my job stays as it is and pay is good.
My real worry is **small shops closing**, not AI.
do: Keep going, using the **translation tool** more.
Check with sales which shops are **in trouble**.
S0.quote: A plateau means more of the same, and after thirty years in homeware I know exactly how to do more of the same.
fieldNote: Thirty years on a **shop floor** gives her a trader's calm.
Her bigger worry is customers going under, not technology.
Steady adaptability shows in sensible small steps.

steps.text: Use the translation tool for all supplier emails abroad
Keep buying colours and ranges for the independent shops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. This one is called Steady Disruption. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real and it'll change office jobs first. At work I'd say let's see which parts help. I'd say among friends that it's coming for everyone's desk, not just mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm a bit uneasy. Listing, comparing and checking prices are things software does well. I'm the junior, so Beatrice's job is safer, and mine is the one they could thin. I'll let the software list the sofas, but I want a human to decide which supplier is allowed to ship late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new tools properly, with proof first that they work. I'd ask Mr Halloran, our boss, about the plan for the buying team. And I'd keep a record of the deals I've made that no software would have found.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a long tide, not a wave. I can live with that. I'd keep my cushion in mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd worry about the young buyer, Daniel. He's good with the tools, but he's treated as if he's cheap. Someone with his skills should get paid for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What parts of your day feel safest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the hands-on stuff, like opening a sample box and feeling the stitching, stays human for longer. That's why I'd keep a small bit of every day for that.

say: I'd say it's real and hits **office jobs first**.
Among friends I'd say it's coming for **everyone's desk**.
think: Listing and price-checking suit software, so my job could be **thinned**.
I'm a bit **uneasy**, and Beatrice's job looks safer than mine.
do: Learn the new tools **properly**, after seeing proof they work.
Ask Mr Halloran about the **plan** for buyers.
Keep a record of **deals** software wouldn't have found.
feel: A **long tide**, not a wave, which I can live with.
S1.quote: I'll let the software list the sofas, but I want a human to decide which supplier is allowed to ship late.
fieldNote: Reads her **junior status** as the weak spot, with Beatrice protected.
Plans a record of human-only wins to use as evidence.
Likes hands-on sample checking as a protected part of her day.

steps.text: Learn the new buying tools after seeing proof they work
Ask Mr Halloran about the plan for the buying team
Keep a log of supplier deals software would have missed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. This one is called AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is very short. At work I'd say we need a straight answer from Mr Halloran. To friends I'd say get your savings in order and stay calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm anxious. Almost all of what I do is screen work, and I'm junior at 58. Two years is short enough to scare me and long enough to stop me pretending, so I'd plan for the worst and hope for less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the extras, like the monthly shopping trips and the gym I never use. I'd put money into the pension and clear the little debt we have. And I'd ask Oakfield about leaving at 60 on decent terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels heavy, but I'd sleep. I'm the type who makes a list and gets on. The list helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Marcus's job affect your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marcus works in a pharmacy, and I think pharmacy shelves and dispensing are partly hands-on, so he has more time than me. That's a comfort. We'd lean on his wage if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tiago and Lia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also have a talk with Tiago and Lia, because they might think our money is theirs. I'd keep a lump aside for their weddings, but the rest is ours.

say: I'd say two years is **very short** and we need straight answers.
To friends I'd say get your **savings** in order.
think: Most of what I do is screen work, so I'm **anxious**.
I'd plan for the **worst** and hope for less.
do: Cut extras like **shopping trips** and the unused gym.
Put money into the **pension** and clear small debts.
Ask Oakfield about **leaving at 60** on decent terms.
feel: **Heavy**, but the lists keep me going.
S2.quote: Two years is short enough to scare me and long enough to stop me pretending, so I'd plan for the worst and hope for less.
fieldNote: Turns fear into **lists**, which keeps her functioning.
Marcus's partly hands-on pharmacy job gives her a **buffer**.
Wants to protect some money for the children's big days.

steps.text: Cancel the gym and the monthly shopping trips
Put extra into the pension and clear the small debts
Ask Oakfield about leaving at 60 on decent terms
Set aside a fixed sum for Tiago and Lia's big days

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. This one is called AGI by 2031. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan but not to relax. At work I'd say watch what the company does. Online I'd say everyone should check their pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm uneasy. By 2031 I'm 63, and I'll be near the end of my working life. With five years I'd keep my head down, save hard and decide at 61 whether to leave or stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work, save and learn the AI helper better, to be useful. I'd look into part-time options so I could taper. I'd keep in touch with the independent shops, who like me and might hire me as an adviser.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels manageable. I'd like to be the one who chooses the end date, and five years lets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter Lia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Lia, who has a mortgage, to build a rainy-day fund and not to rely on a single employer. It's the one thing I'd press her on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if a package came early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a package came early, I'd think hard but probably take it. A good ending beats a long wait.

say: I'd say five years is **enough to plan** but not to relax.
Online I'd tell people to **check their pensions**.
think: By 2031 I'm **63**, near the end of working life.
I'd like to be the one who **chooses** my end date.
do: Work, save and learn the **AI helper** better.
Stay close to the shops as a possible **adviser**.
feel: **Manageable**, since five years lets me pick the end date.
S3.quote: With five years I'd keep my head down, save hard and decide at 61 whether to leave or stay.
fieldNote: Time gives her **choice** over the exit.
Sees her shop contacts as a route to part-time advice work.
Presses her daughter to build a rainy-day fund.

steps.text: Save hard for three years and review at 61
Get better at the AI helper for supplier mail
Offer buying advice to independent shops part-time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. This one is called AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is fine for anyone who prepares. At work I'd say train the younger ones. Online I'd say governments should publish plans early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm calm for me. Ten years means my retirement happens first, so my worry is for my daughter Lia, who has just bought a flat. It's the young ones who face it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd retire at 64 or 65 as planned. I'd keep using the translation tool and AI helper a bit, and help the younger buyers. I'd also keep a little money for Lia and Tiago in case it gets tough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels fine and a bit sad. I'd be proud of the work I did but glad to be out of the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with your time after work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend time with grandchildren if there are any, and travel with Marcus. We've always said Portugal and the lakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you want to be remembered at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the interest in homeware going. Maybe volunteering at the charity shop, which would be a nice end to the thirty years on the shop floor.

say: I'd say ten years is **fine** for anyone who prepares.
I'd say governments should publish **plans early**.
At work I'd say train the younger buyers first.
think: I'm **calm** for myself since I'll retire first.
My worry is for my daughter **Lia**, who just bought a flat.
do: Help the **younger buyers** and keep using the helper.
Keep some money aside for **Lia and Tiago**.
feel: **Fine** and a bit sad, proud of the work.
S4.quote: Ten years means my retirement happens first, so my worry is for my daughter Lia, who has just bought a flat.
fieldNote: Her calm is **personal**, her worry family-wide.
Pictures a gentle retirement: travel and a charity shop.
Sees helping younger buyers as her legacy, and wants to leave work on a good note.

steps.text: Keep a sum aside for Lia and Tiago if times get hard
Volunteer at the charity shop after retiring

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's no time to adjust and almost everything I do is screen work. What would help is honest notice from the company, a fair way out at 60, and training that's more than a leaflet. Also clear dates and plans from governments.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people want nuance, not a side. I'm not a fan or a doomsayer, I just want a date, a plan and someone honest telling me what it means for my pension.

headlineQuote: I'm not a fan or a doomsayer, I just want a date, a plan and someone honest telling me what it means for my pension.
portrait: **Yara Santos**, 58, a junior buyer of furniture and homeware at Oakfield, after thirty years on a shop floor.
She is **pragmatic** and middle-of-the-road, and uses a translation tool and AI helper now and then.
Strong savings and Marcus's partly hands-on pharmacy job give her **options**, but her own work is screen work.
Her moods run calm, uneasy and **anxious** only in the 2-year case.
biggestWorry: The **2028 case**, since there is no time to adjust and her work is screen-based.
whatWouldHelp: **Honest notice** and a fair way out at 60.
Training that is **more than a leaflet** and clear dates from governments.
